### G7 — the finding that makes this urgent

**We hold the WRONG DIRECTION across most of Indiana.**

| RTO | injection (generator) | withdrawal (**what a data centre needs**) |
|---|---|---|
| **MISO** | ✅ 642 located Indiana buses | ❌ **NOT HELD** |
| **PJM** | ❌ **NOT HELD** | ✅ 1,475 buses, only **229 located** |

Measured 2026-08-17: `energy.pjm_queuescope_results` is **WITHDRAWAL-only at `desired_mw=100`
across all 24 PJM transmission owners** — there is no injection hiding in it to clip. And most of
Indiana is MISO (Duke Energy Indiana 881k customers, IPL 519k, NIPSCO 486k); PJM here is
essentially I&M (608k). **So for the majority of the state we hold only the generator direction.**

⛔ **Injection headroom is NOT a weaker version of withdrawal headroom — it is a different
question.** A 5,000 MW injection figure says nothing about whether a 300 MW load can be served.
Never average, compare or substitute across the two. `direction` rides on every bus row in
`export_grid_siting.py` for exactly this reason. Agent is permitted to return **BLOCKED with a
verbatim wall** on the MISO-withdrawal half — MISO's `poi_mf` API is a *generator* tool and a
public load-side equivalent may simply not exist.

**Measured consequence, 2026-08-17:** of 532,868 screener candidates, **only 207,614 (39%) have any
load-side bus within 25 miles**, while 515,932 (97%) have an injection bus. For three fifths of the
candidate set, *the direction a data centre actually needs is unavailable.*

#### G7b — the request-size ladder (operator, 2026-08-17)

**Headroom is a FUNCTION of the request size, and we harvested exactly one rung per direction:**
MISO injection at `pMaxValue=300` only; PJM withdrawal at `desired_mw=100` only. A bus with 800 MW
free to a 100 MW request may have far less free to a 1,000 MW request — and a hyperscale campus is
a 300–1,000 MW ask. **A single-proxy answer misrepresents precisely the size class this application
exists to serve.**

Ladder to acquire: **100 / 300 / 500 / 1000 / 2500 / 5000 MW**, for BOTH directions, BOTH RTOs —
6 × 2 × 2 = up to 24 cells. Deliverable is a **cell-by-cell LANDED / BLOCKED / not-offered matrix**
in `docs/RTO_DIRECTIONS.md`; partial coverage is expected and fine. Request size must be a COLUMN
(`request_mw`), never one table per size, so the existing 300 and 100 rungs fold in rather than
duplicate. Sent to the in-flight agent as a scope extension.

### G13 — voltage: filter by it, colour by it, and AUDIT it (operator, 2026-08-17)

*"The substations/buses/transmission lines should also be filterable by kV and the transmission
lines should depict different colors based on their voltage — some mislabeled and should be
audited/fixed."*

Three separate pieces of work, and **the third is the one that matters most**:

1. **Filter by voltage** on substations, connection points (buses) and transmission lines. The
   screener already filters substations by kV; the map console does not filter any of the three.
2. **Colour transmission lines by voltage class**, the way the operator's own Illinois dashboard
   does. Today all lines render one colour, so a 765 kV backbone and a 69 kV lateral look identical
   — and they are not remotely the same siting fact.
3. ⚠ **Audit the voltage labels first.** Operator reports some are mislabeled. `in_transmission_union`
   is a HIFLD+OSM merge carrying `voltage_raw`, `kv` and `volt_class`, and the two publishers
   disagree about units and encoding (volts vs kilovolts, ranges, nulls). **Colouring by a field
   that is wrong just renders the error in high contrast** — and a mislabeled voltage propagates
   into the substation kV filter the screener already ships. Measure the `kv` distribution against
   `voltage_raw` per source, quantify the disagreement, then fix, then colour.

⛔ Do not treat an unknown voltage as 0 — `in_substations` already has blank-is-unknown handling and
"never treated as 0" is the standing rule. An unknown-voltage line needs its own colour, not the
bottom of the scale.

### G9 — date-gate the signals, but ONLY the ones that are events (operator, 2026-08-17)

*"We should really only take the SI events after Jan 2020, so the signals that are time-dependent,
and maintain the within-X-days filter... however, a remediation site will always be a remediation
site and a vacant property — parcel without a building — will likely always stay that way."*

**The distinction this creates, which the corpus does not currently make:**

| kind | behaviour | date gate? |
|---|---|---|
| **EVENT signals** — a thing happened on a date | goes stale. A 2014 foreclosure says nothing about today's owner | ✅ **cut before 2020-01-01**, keep the within-X-days filter |
| **STATE signals** — a standing condition | does not go stale. Contamination does not expire; a delisted plant stays delisted | ❌ **no date gate** — gating these would silently delete real, current inventory |

Classification to apply (from the measured 18-code vocabulary):
- **EVENT:** tax sale, tax delinquency, foreclosure, code violation, unsafe building, vacant board
  order, demolition order, structure fire, environmental violation, assessment appeal, loan
  maturity, SBA charge-off, mass-layoff notice
- **STATE:** brownfield / remediation, facility inactive, plant delisting, government surplus,
  abandoned building *(argue this one — an abandonment record is a finding, not a dated event)*

⚠ Measure the loss before shipping the cut, and report it: a date gate that removes most of the
corpus is a decision, not a filter, and 69% of the environmental corpus is already known to be more
than ten years old.

#### MEASURED 2026-08-17 — and the naive cut would have been destructive

27,711 signal attachments across 24,275 parcels:

| | attachments | share |
|---|---:|---:|
| latest event **2020 or later** | 11,491 | 41.5% |
| latest event **before 2020** | 6,396 | 23.1% |
| **UNDATED** | **9,824** | **35.5%** |

⛔ **A `last_event >= '2020-01-01'` predicate silently drops all 9,824 undated rows**, because
`NULL >= DATE` evaluates to NULL, not TRUE. That is the *"unpublished is NULL, never 0"* rule wearing
a new costume, and it would have looked like a clean 41.5% filter.

**Worse, it lands hardest on the biggest signal.** `D4_tax_delinquency` is the largest signal we
hold — 9,459 parcels — and **8,523 of them (90%) carry no date at all.** A post-2020 cut would
delete nine tenths of it *not because the delinquency is old but because we never captured a date.*
`D7_brownfield` is 263 undated of 311, and it is a STATE signal that must not be gated regardless.

**So the gate is THREE-WAY, not two-way:**

| case | treatment |
|---|---|
| EVENT signal, dated | apply the cut |
| **EVENT signal, undated** | **`recency unknown` — surfaced as itself, never silently dropped.** The user chooses whether to include it |
| STATE signal | never gated |

Follow-on finding worth its own item: **90% of our largest signal is undated.** That is an
acquisition gap, not a display problem — `D4` dates are the highest-value date work left.

### G10 — "vacant" currently means two different things, and nothing distinguishes them

Operator, 2026-08-17: *"we need to clarify the distinction between vacancy as a parcel without a
building and an actually abandoned building (the actual signal). This is not recognized
throughout."* **Correct, and the screener I built today commits the error on one screen:** a filter
reading *"Vacant land (nothing built on it)"* sits feet away from a signal named
`D5_vacant_board_order`, which is about a **building**. One word, two unrelated meanings, no cue.

Binding resolution — one word, one meaning:

| concept | the ONLY term to use | never call it |
|---|---|---|
| a parcel carrying no structure (a land attribute, **not** a signal, and not distress at all) | **undeveloped land** | vacant, vacant land, empty |
| a **building** that stands empty / boarded / abandoned (a real owner-motivation signal) | **vacant building** / **abandoned building** | vacant land, vacancy |

Also affects: `has_vacancy_signal` in `in_sites`, the `f-vac` control on the map console, the
`site_kind` vocabulary, and every "vacant" string in `si.html`. Sweep all of them.

### G8 — the binding translation table

**Rule: a label a user cannot decode is a broken feature, however correct the number behind it.**
Internal codenames stay in the code, the docs and the registry. They do NOT appear in the UI.

| we say internally | the user sees | why ours fails |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | **Owner motivation** — *is this owner likely to sell?* | "P1" names a slot in our build order, not a concept |
| P2 | **Power & grid** | |
| P3 | **Land & size** | already plain — keep |
| P4 | **Environmental constraints** | |
| P5 | **Community & local rules** | |
| P6 | **Market & cost** | |
| P7 | **State legislation** | |
| SI / SI Feed / seller-intent signal | **Owner-motivation signals** | "SI" is an acronym for an acronym |
| D4, D12, D22 … | the signal's plain name — *tax delinquency*, *code violation*, *environmental violation* | a code is not a name |
| class union | **screened sites** | set-theory vocabulary in a UI |
| occ_group = 'ci' | **commercial / industrial** | a database enum |
| cannot assess | **not measured here** (+ *"left out of the score, never counted as zero"*) | reads as a system failure rather than a coverage statement |
| denominator | **how many sites we counted** | |
| posture_renderable / evidence_grade | **verified at an official source** vs **reported, not yet verified** | our gating vocabulary, not the reader's question |
| fan-out, D85, parcel_source | never surfaced at all | internal integrity machinery |

## OPERATOR RULINGS — 2026-08-16, binding

**R1. KEEP EVERY PARCEL. Do not filter the rendered payload by occupancy class.**
The proposal was to drop parcels carrying a residential structure, on the grounds that a house
cannot host a hyperscale DC or a 5 MW BESS. Measured before acting, that cut would have removed
**165,003 parcels of which 160,669 fit a 25 MW datacentre** — because `occ_group` describes the
STRUCTURE, not the land, and 97.5% of them are **farmsteads**: 5–20 ac (87,541), 20–100 ac
(63,310), 100+ ac (9,953, largest **6,374 acres**), averaging 3–5 structures. A farmhouse on 200
acres classes residential and is exactly the site a developer wants.
Only 4,199 were genuine small lots — **0.35% of the 1.2M payload**, no meaningful performance win.
**Operator ruling: keep them all, because a 250 kW or 500 kW BESS may be installed later** and
needs a fraction of the land 5 MW does. Capability columns (`fits_min_bess_5mw`, `fits_dc_25mw`)
already filter on what the land can hold, which is the question that actually matters.

**R2. Vacant land stays** — 896,947 no-structure parcels, unchanged. (Restates the standing rule.)

**R3. STRUCTURAL DISTRESS MUST PLAUSIBLY PRODUCE INTENT. A minor incident does not.**
Operator, 2026-08-16. Applied to the 910,483-row Indianapolis code corpus as a two-tier gate
rather than a case-type list:
- **Tier 1, admitted on a single occurrence** — Unsafe Buildings, Vacant Board Order, Demolition.
  Each already means the building is unusable.
- **Tier 2, admitted only where chronic or unresolved** — Building violations, Repair orders,
  Environmental. Measured: **16,325 addresses have exactly one structural case; 2,176 have ten or
  more.** One citation is an incident; ten is an owner who has stopped maintaining the property.
- **Excluded outright regardless of type:** `Closed, No Violation` (60,449) and `Void` (13,987) —
  an inspector finding nothing is not distress, and counting it would be the "0 high-priority
  violators" error inverted.
- Also excluded, counted not dropped: High Weeds & Grass **363,844**, Trash 103,792, Zoning
  225,359, Vehicle 46,969. Admitting the corpus wholesale would have inflated D12 by ~750,000
  rows of lawn care — the South Bend error a third time.

## ⛔ WHERE THE DATA LIVES — read this before "rebuilding" anything

**Our data lives in `energy-platfrom.indiana_app`. All of it. There is nothing of ours in
`energy`.** The checkpoint proves it: `0 tables named in_* exist in energy`.

**The thing that confuses people** (it confused the author of this file): 157 of our 268 registered
objects record `energy.*` as their **SOURCE**. That is *provenance, not storage*. `in_sites` is a
table in `indiana_app`; `energy.vw_parcel_sites` is where its rows came from. Reading that source
field as "our data is in energy" leads straight to someone rebuilding a table we already hold.

**The dependency, measured by `scripts/checkpoint.py` on every run:**

| | |
|---|---|
| BUILD scripts that read `energy` | **65** — expected and correct; this is how clips are made |
| EXPORTS that read `energy` | **0** — enforced by a checkpoint check that FAILS if one appears |
| tables we created inside `energy` | **0** |
| writes to `energy` | APPEND-only rows to `energy.registry_sources`, the single permitted exception |

**Build scripts may read `energy`. Exports may not.** An export is on the path to what the user
sees, so the app must be rebuildable from `indiana_app` alone. The one violation
(`export_spine.py` counting unplottable SI rows live) was closed by clipping the slice into
`in_si_plottability` and reading that.

### Should we duplicate the ~140 energy source tables? **No.**

1. **The data we need is already here.** The clips ARE the duplication, already done, already
   Indiana-only, already registered.
2. **The sources are national and enormous.** `mat_parcel_attrs` is 107M rows, `cems_hourly` 36M,
   `mat_si_plottable` 80M+. Copying them whole to obtain an Indiana slice we already hold would
   cost storage and buy nothing.
3. **It would collide with the national buildout**, which owns those tables and rebuilds them.
4. **The correct pattern is the one already in use:** clip the slice, register it in the same run,
   and read the clip. `in_si_plottability` is the worked example — a national 80M-row table
   reduced to the four numbers Indiana actually needs.

**If a future session finds itself about to rebuild something because it saw `energy.x` in a
script: stop and check `docs/TABLE_INVENTORY.md` first.** All 269 objects are listed there.

| script | asks | catches |

| `scripts/audit_honesty.py` | is what we ship true? | 13 adversarial checks incl. **payload vs warehouse**, D85 in any spatial join, a cannot-assess shipped as 0, and **every committed loader having a table** |
| `scripts/audit_wiring_census.py` | does every registered object reach a surface? | the denominator MOVES on every build — never quote a past figure |

**The "is it current" check earned its place the hard way.** The map showed 4 ordinances while the
warehouse held 153 candidates, 19 admitted and 73 verified county actions. Nothing errored; the
page rendered what it was told, and what it was told was two generations old. Every other check
asked "does it work".

## RULES EARNED THIS SESSION

1. **A completeness shortfall must be an `assert`, not a `print`.** The sweep loader reported "79 of 92" to a console nobody re-read and would have loaded anyway.
2. **An agent's deliverable is a file IT writes.** A parent collecting sub-agent replies lost 13 counties once and a whole NW pass entirely.
3. **For a scraper, "committed" and "safe" are different properties.** `.gitignore` excludes `scrapers/**/*.json` by design, so only the warehouse proves the second.
4. **A generated document must not carry hand-typed claims.** `SI_COVERAGE.md` asserted D4 absent for a whole session. Every NOT-HELD claim now carries a build-time probe; unprobed claims print as UNVERIFIED.
5. **Read the console in a fresh tab, or not at all.** A reused tab accumulates your own probes and reads as page defects.
6. **Check the state slice, not the national number.** `mat_parcel_attrs` has 69M owner names and **zero** for `parcel_source='parcels_in'`.
7. **Never assume a date format.** A `%Y-%m-%d` parse over `MM/DD/YYYY` reported "0 upcoming auctions" when 16,325 were upcoming; the corrected parse then threw on `00/00/0000` and needed `SAFE.PARSE_DATE`.
8. `r.keys` collides with `Row.keys()` — **third recorded occurrence**. Alias it `n_keys`.
9. **An audit that cries wolf gets ignored.** `audit_frontend.py` opened with 56 findings and
   roughly zero real ones. Four false-positive classes had to go before it was worth reading:
   runtime-created ids, brace-depth vs indentation, template-literal ids (`` $(`w-${k}`) ``, which
   reported the entire scoring UI as dead), and property scanning inside string literals. Same
   failure as the wiring census counting build scripts as features.
10. **"Does it work" and "is it current" are different questions.** A page can be perfectly
    functional and two generations out of date, with no error anywhere.
11. **A wall is an observation, not a property of a host.** Four robots-403 walls did not
    reproduce on re-test. Re-check a BLOCKED record before treating it as final — including
    amlegal, which currently gates 17 counties.
12. **A disagreement between two instruments means at least one is wrong.** It is not a tie to
    break by preference. Both NW sweeps reported Jasper PC-22-25 as verified; both were wrong.
13. **Distance is not the test for a coordinate — the PARCEL is.** Five of six pin offsets were
    cosmetic; the sixth put a data centre on the wrong side of the street and the wrong parcel.
14. **Never guess a column name, including in a throwaway probe.** Cost four separate zero-result
    queries this session: `ADDRESS_ID` for `FULL_ADDRESS`, `geog` for `lat`/`lon`, `facility_name`
    then `already_pinned_as` (which carries coordinates in parentheses).
15. **ASCII in console output.** cp1252 cannot encode `≈ → ✗ ↔ ⚠`, and three scripts died on
    their own `print()` — including the honesty audit crashing on its FAILURE path. 44 scripts now
    reconfigure stdout; keep new ones ASCII or add the shim.
16. **Use a commit-message FILE.** Backticks and double quotes in `-m` get eaten by the shell.
17. **A coverage field records ONE pass, not the state of the world.**
    `in_dc_actions_coverage_v2.official_site_fetched` reads `'False'` for **50 counties**, which
    reads as "we never checked". For **32 of them the official source WAS subsequently reached**,
    by the verification pass in `in_dc_actions_resolved` — every one of the 32 has a verification
    verdict, 21 carry a `VERIFIED_AT_OFFICIAL_SOURCE` row that renders and 11 were verified and
    then **suppressed**. Zero unverified claims render. That stale field is what generated F1/F2 as
    phantom open work. **Ask the table that gates rendering (`posture_renderable`), never the
    table that logged the first sweep.**
18. **Two open items describing one job will both survive an audit.** F1 and F2 were written as
    separate follow-ups from separate observations; measured, they are the *same 18-county
    re-sweep*, which had already run. A ledger dedupes by *work*, not by wording.

## TYPE TRAPS IN THIS WAREHOUSE — read before writing a WHERE clause

Booleans are **not** consistently BOOL across our own tables, and guessing costs a query each time:

| table | column | actual type | correct predicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| `in_dc_actions_coverage_v2` | `official_site_fetched` | **STRING** `'True'`/`'False'` | `= "False"` |
| `in_dc_actions_resweep_coverage` | `official_site_fetched` | **STRING** | `= "True"` |
| `in_dc_actions_resolved` | `posture_renderable` | **BOOL** | `COUNTIF(posture_renderable)` |

`IS TRUE` against the STRING columns fails with *"No matching signature for operator IS TRUE"*, and
`= "True"` against the BOOL fails with *"BOOL, STRING"*. Both happened on 2026-08-17. Rule 14 said
never guess a column NAME; this extends it: **never guess its TYPE either — `get_table().schema`
costs nothing.** Note also that `get_table().num_rows` is **0 for every view** — that is metadata,
not emptiness. `COUNT(*)` the views.
